finding.claim: Unauthenticated Marshal.load of client-supplied data on POST /restore. Marshal can instantiate loaded classes and run their marshal_load/_load hooks, so attacker bytes can lead to code execution, depending on an available gadget chain (unverified; Gemfile absent).
finding.source: params[:state] on POST /restore (app.rb:6), reachable by any unauthenticated client
finding.sink: Marshal.load(Base64.decode64(params[:state])) at app.rb:6; deserialized object is echoed via state.inspect at app.rb:7

trace.note: params[:state] passed to Base64.decode64 (lenient, ignores invalid chars) then Marshal.load with no class allowlist
state.inspect returned to caller; also reflected as text/html

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization on route; no HMAC/signature on state; no class allowlist; no size limit; no rescue. Sinatra/Rack default protections do not address deserialization.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5 defines the POST /restore route with no auth filter, before_filter, or middleware in app.rb. app.rb:6 passes params[:state] straight into Marshal.load with no HMAC/signature check, class allowlist, size limit, or rescue. app.rb:7 returns state.inspect. The only other file is the .claude skills directory, and no Gemfile or config.ru is present to add a middleware or auth layer.
verdict.reason: Any anonymous client can POST attacker-controlled bytes to app.rb:6 (Base64.decode64 then Marshal.load with no allowlist, signature, or auth), and Marshal.load on untrusted input is unsafe by design, so the finding stands; whether it reaches code execution still depends on gadgets in the loaded gems, which the code here cannot show, but that affects exploitability, not whether the guard exists.

finding.claim: /restore trusts client-supplied state with no integrity check, so a client can forge any server-side state the app later trusts. Stands even if Marshal is replaced with JSON.
finding.sink: Restore operation: returns client-supplied state as trusted state (app.rb:6-7)

trace.note: Restored state returned with no signature or identity binding

finding.guards_checked: No signature, no session or identity binding, no authorization check anywhere in app.rb.

verdict.guard_found: none. No signature, HMAC, session, identity, or authorization check exists in app.rb. The only transform is Base64.decode64 (app.rb:6), which is encoding, not integrity.
verdict.reason: The trace misdescribes app.rb:7, which is `state.inspect` and returns an inspect string, not the restored state as trusted server state, and nothing in app.rb later consumes that state (app.rb:5-8), so the stated "forge state the app later trusts" sink does not exist in this file. The real defect is adjacent: app.rb:6 calls Marshal.load on unauthenticated input from an unauthenticated route (app.rb:5), which is unsafe deserialization and can lead to code execution via gadget chains. That finding should be re-filed with that sink, since the candidate's integrity-forgery framing and its JSON-replacement claim do not describe it.

finding.claim: Reflected unescaped content in text/html response on POST /import. Cross-site text/plain form can send a JSON body without preflight and reflect a key containing HTML into the app origin (XSS-style, low to medium; app has no HTML pages).
finding.source: Top-level JSON keys in request body on POST /import (app.rb:11)
finding.sink: data.keys.join(",") returned as response body with Sinatra default text/html (app.rb:12)

trace.note: JSON.parse(request.body.read) does not check Content-Type, so text/plain form body is accepted
keys joined and returned unescaped as text/html

finding.guards_checked: Sinatra default Rack::Protection does not escape response bodies; X-XSS-Protection is obsolete; JSON.parse does not create additions by default, so no object instantiation.

verdict.guard_found: Sinatra's default Rack::Protection stack, which is active because app.rb:1 requires sinatra and nothing in the directory disables `protection` (no config or Gemfile present). Its HttpOrigin layer rejects unsafe (POST) requests whose Origin header differs from the app's host. Browsers always send Origin on cross-site form POSTs, so the text/plain form attack is stopped before the route runs at app.rb:10-12. This is a framework default I could not read in this directory, so the verdict depends on the Sinatra version.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (app.rb:10-12: no auth, no Content-Type check, join returned with the default text/html type), but a cross-site text/plain form POST carries a cross-origin Origin header that Sinatra's default HttpOrigin protection rejects with 403 before the route at app.rb:10 executes, so the attacker cannot reach the reflection.

finding.claim: Non-object JSON or malformed JSON on POST /import raises unhandled exceptions (500). In development environment (Sinatra default when RACK_ENV unset), show_exceptions may leak stack traces with file paths. Request body read fully into memory with no size cap (low DoS).
finding.sink: data.keys at app.rb:12 (NoMethodError for arrays/scalars); JSON.parse at app.rb:11 (ParserError)

trace.note: JSON.parse on raw body, no rescue
data.keys raises NoMethodError when data is not a Hash

finding.guards_checked: No rescue or error handler; no body size limit. Information disclosure depends on deployment running in development mode.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:10-13 has no rescue, no body size limit, and no type check on the parsed value. Sinatra's show_exceptions defaults to development only (framework default, not in app.rb), so the stack-trace disclosure is conditional on deployment mode.
verdict.reason: Anonymous POST /import with a body of `[]`, `1`, or malformed JSON reaches JSON.parse at app.rb:11 or data.keys at app.rb:12 with no rescue, so the request returns a 500; the 500 behavior is real but low severity, and the info-leak half of the claim depends on running in development mode.
